bib.title: Wizard of Wikipedia: Knowledge-Powered Conversational agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Wizard of Wikipedia: Knowledge-Powered Conversational Agents", Emily Dinan, Stephen Roller, Kurt Shuster (joint first), Angela Fan, Michael Auli, Jason Weston (Facebook AI Research). ICLR 2019. arXiv:1811.01241v2, 21 Feb 2019.

COVERAGE: I read all 59,189 of 59,189 extracted characters, covering all 18 pages, including the appendices and Tables 6–8. I skimmed the references. Appendix headings A.1 (wizard UI image), B.2 and B.3 have no body text in the extraction, so they are probably image or table pointers only.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: Generation depends on picking the right knowledge. Given the gold sentence a human chose, the generative models score about twice the F1 they get when they must pick knowledge themselves.
  number: E2E (w/ aux loss) Test Seen F1 16.9 with predicted knowledge vs 35.5 with gold; Unseen 14.4 vs 32.2
  setup: Table 4. Generative Transformer MemNet, full Wizard task. Unigram F1 against the gold response. Retrieval is TF-IDF IR (top 7 articles x 3 queries).
  quote: "E2E Transformer MemNet (w/ auxiliary loss) 63.5 16.9 97.3 14.4 23.1 35.5 32.8 32.2"
  where: p7, Table 4

- claim: Picking the knowledge is hard on its own. The best model picks the sentence the human wizard used about a quarter of the time, and plain IR does barely better than random.
  number: R@1 25.5 seen / 22.9 unseen (Transformer +Reddit +SQuAD); IR baseline 5.8 / 7.6; random 2.7 / 2.3
  setup: Table 2. Knowledge Selection Task, test split, roughly 61 candidates per turn.
  quote: "Transformer (+Reddit pretraining, +SQuAD training) 25.5 36.2 22.9 34.2" / "IR baseline 5.8 21.8 7.6 23.5"
  where: p6, Table 2 (candidate count: p13, "giving∼61 knowledge candidates per turn")

- claim: Pretraining decides whether a selector generalises to unseen topics. Without Reddit pretraining the Transformer drops to 12.2 R@1 on unseen topics; with it, 23.7.
  number: 22.5→12.2 seen→unseen (no pretrain) vs 24.5→23.7 (Reddit)
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "Transformers work best, as long as they are pretrained on a large dataset (Reddit), while multi-tasking on SQuAD provides marginal impact."
  where: p6

- claim: Adding knowledge improves every retrieval (response-ranking) model.
  number: BoW MemNet 56 to 71 R@1; Transformer 79 to 87 R@1 (Test Seen, predicted knowledge)
  setup: Table 3. Rank the gold response among 99 random candidates.
  quote: "improving Bow MemNet from 56 to 71 R@1 and the Transformer MemNet from 79 to 87 R@1) for predicted knowledge"
  where: p6

- claim: In human evaluation, retrieval models were rated more engaging than generative ones, and knowledge made the generative models significantly more engaging and much more knowledgeable (Wiki F1).
  number: Two-Stage Generative MemNet rating 2.92 seen / 2.93 unseen, Wiki F1 30.0 / 26.2; Generative no-knowledge 2.11 / 2.54, Wiki F1 15.3 / 10.1; Retrieval MemNet 3.43 / 3.14; humans 4.13 / 4.34
  setup: Table 5. Engagingness rated 1–5 after 3–5 turns; 546 conversations, 464 workers. Wiki F1 is unigram overlap with the first 10 sentences of the topic's Wikipedia page.
  quote: "For the generative models, we find human engagingness ratings are significantly improved by the use of knowledge (p < .01)." / "Two-Stage Generative Transformer MemNet 2.92 (1.33) 30.0 2.93 (1.30) 26.2"
  where: p8, Table 5 and text

- claim: The retrieval-versus-generative gap in knowledge shown widens on unseen topics, because retrieval models can only return training-set utterances.
  number: none
  setup: Table 5, unseen split
  quote: "retrieval models are limited to producing a response from the training set where the unseen topic did not appear."
  where: p9

- claim: Splitting selection from generation (Two-stage) wins with predicted knowledge. End-to-end wins with gold knowledge. The auxiliary knowledge loss and knowledge dropout both help.
  number: Two-stage w/ K.D. PPL 46.5, F1 18.9 seen (predicted) vs E2E 63.5, 16.9
  setup: Table 4
  quote: "This suggests that the Two-stage model benefits from the strong knowledge selection module (Section 5.1), but that the End-to-end model is better at employing the selected knowledge."
  where: p7

- claim: Grounded models still produce fluent factual errors. The knowledge-grounded retriever confuses topics on unseen data, and the generator gets dates and names wrong.
  number: none
  setup: Appendix C error analysis. 20 sampled conversations per setting, single-blind.
  quote: "Frequently in unseen topics, the retriever with knowledge produces similar, but factually inaccurate answers to user queries. For example, when one user asks about parts of Ireland to visit, the model enumerates a list of locations in Greece." / "it sometimes produces statements using an incorrect date, name or word"
  where: p15–16

- claim: Knowledge reduces the repetition typical of seq2seq models, but it does so by copying Wikipedia, and the result is formulaic.
  number: none
  quote: "The generator with knowledge has significantly fewer issues with repetition, as it errs on the side of copying large fragments from the Wikipedia knowledge."
  where: p15

- claim: Dataset scale and split. Test Unseen has 58 topics not seen in train or validation. The knowledge base is all of Wikipedia.
  number: 22,311 dialogues, 201,999 turns; 1,365 topics; 5.4M articles / 93M sentences; wizards chose "no sentence used" 6.2% of the time
  quote: "The final dialogue dataset we collect consists of 22,311 dialogues with 201,999 turns, which we divide into 166,787 for train, 17,715 for validation, and 17,497 for test." / "Knowledge Database 5.4M articles 93M sentences"
  where: p4, Table 1; p13

- claim: The retriever is the fixed DrQA TF-IDF retriever. It is queried separately for the topic and each of the last two turns, and the results are flattened into title-prefixed sentences.
  number: top 7 articles per query, 3 queries
  quote: "effectively calling the IR system three times with three different queries. Empirically, this provided better performance compared to merging into one query"
  where: p4

LIMITS:
- The paper measures no hallucination rate. Factual errors appear only in anecdotes: the starred lines in Figures 4–5 and the Appendix C sample of 20 conversations. Wiki F1 measures overlap, not correctness, and the authors concede it can be gamed ("a model could display knowledge by copying parts of Wikipedia, but not be engaging at all", p8 fn1).
- The retrieval step is fixed TF-IDF IR. A learned retriever is listed as future work ("learning to retrieve and reason simultaneously rather than using a separate IR component", p9).
- Every model remains well below human engagingness (p9).
- Human evaluation ran only 3–5 turns on a 1–5 "liked" scale. The human-human baseline differs from the dataset setup because neither human acted as wizard (p14).
- This is 2018 work: small Transformers, response ranking against training utterances, no LLMs. The absolute numbers are out of date. The benchmark and the gap between gold and predicted knowledge are what still apply.

BUILDS ON: End-to-end Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015); Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017); the DrQA/Open-SQuAD TF-IDF retriever (Chen et al., 2017); Reddit pretraining (Mazaré et al., 2018); in-batch negatives (Henderson et al., 2017); BPE (Sennrich et al., 2016); sentence normalisation (Cer et al., 2018); topics from Persona-Chat (Zhang et al., 2018); knowledge-grounded dialogue predecessors (Ghazvininejad et al., 2018; Parthasarathi & Pineau, 2018; Dodge et al., 2016); Wizard-of-Oz collection (Bernsen et al., 2012). The authors present knowledge dropout as their own technique, related to feature dropout (Wu et al., 2017).

CODE: none in the paper. The loss is L = (1−λ)L_NLL + λL_knowledge (p5). The dataset is in ParlAI: http://parl.ai/projects/wizard of wikipedia/ (p2).

FIGURES:
- Figure 1, p5: "Generative Transformer Memory Network. An IR system provides knowledge candidates from Wikipedia. Dialogue Context and Knowledge are encoded using a shared encoder. In the Two-stage model, the dialogue and knowledge are re-encoded after knowledge selection." One diagram shows the retrieve, select, generate split, with the knowledge-selection loss alongside the generation loss. This is the best candidate.
- Figure 4, p17, as an alternative: example conversations from the knowledge-grounded retriever, with factual mistakes starred (the Ireland→Greece case). It shows a grounded model making errors faster than prose would.

FIT WITH NOTES:
- Best fit: 02-why-rag-and-the-augmented-prompt.md, "What RAG buys you" table, "Fewer hallucinations" row (line 111). That row cites Shuster et al. (arXiv:2104.07567) and names Wizard of Wikipedia, but it never cites Dinan et al. This counts as "sharpens": add the Dinan citation as the origin of the benchmark (dataset, seen/unseen split, Wikipedia knowledge base) and add a references row. Nothing in the paper contradicts the note. The paper does not support the 68.2% → 8–21% hallucination figures. Those come from Shuster, and Dinan measures no hallucination rate. Do not attribute any hallucination number to Dinan.
- Second fit: 01-rag-pipeline.md, "Where naive RAG fails" (failure table near line 71) or "Measure each stage" (line 368). The gap between gold and predicted knowledge (F1 16.9 vs 35.5) shows end-quality capped by the selection or retrieval stage, which supports evaluating stages separately. The Appendix C observation that a model grounded in retrieved text can still give confident wrong answers (Ireland→Greece) matches the note's "contextual hallucination" row. The note's FLARE sentence (line 95) mentions Wizard of Wikipedia without a citation, so a Dinan citation could go there as well.
- No contradictions found.

PROBLEMS: The title's first word "WIZARD" was lost in extraction. Small-caps headings came out split (for example "I NTRODUCTION"). The A.1 UI image and the B.2/B.3 sections have no text. I found no embedded instructions.
